newsitem.title: JAPAN: Communists to gain strength in Japan parliament-TV.
newsitem.headline: Communists to gain strength in Japan parliament-TV.

text.p: Japan's communists, capitalising on voter disillusionment with major parties, looked set to increase their seats in parliament after Sunday's general election.

Exit polls by several TV networks shortly after polling closed showed the Japan Communist Party (JCP), which had 15 seats in the outgoing 511-member Lower House, could raise the number to between 25 and 32 in the new 500-seat chamber.
Two and a half hours after the polls closed, the Communists had won at least nine seats, NHK public television said.

Analysts had said voters disenchanted with bigger parties and unhappy with the status quo might vote for the Communists, whose policies could be perceived as more consistent than those of some others during the past three years of turbulence in Japanese politics.

The JCP was also expected to benefit from an anticipated slip in the number of Socialists in parliament. The Social Democratic Party, a junior partner in Japan's coalition government, is struggling amid a split between die-hard leftists and moderate members which has resulted in mass defections.
TV exit polls said the number of Social Democrats in the Lower House could be nearly halved from 30 before the election.
With some polls predicting a coalition as the most likely result, the JCP appeared poised for a new enhanced role.

"If the Communist Party wins more seats, Japan's politics would be plunged into a new form of instability," political analyst Minoru Morita said. "It would spark fear among all the non-Communist parties and prompt them to form an awkward unified front against the Communists," he added.
Senior JCP official Kazuo Shii has said his party planned to woo the "disaffected" and "undecided", which polls indicated numbered more than half of Japan's 98 million voters.
"We are seeking cooperation from both reformists and conservatives who have no allegiance to any political party," he told a news conference earlier this month.
The most seats ever won by the Communists, Japan's oldest party, was 41 in 1979. It fielded 321 candidates this time.

The party lost support in the early 1990s after the Soviet Union collapsed. It bounced back this year to win mayoral elections in two Tokyo suburbs, which analysts had said could be a pointer to Sunday's polls.
In its election platform, the JCP promised to force U.S. troops out of Japan, scrap the Japan-U.S. Security Treaty and nullify a planned rise in the sales tax.

"The government that the general public really needs is one in which citizens, not business circles or the United States, play the leading role," JCP chairman Tetsuzo Fuwa said in a recent campaign speech.
The rape of a schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen in Okinawa last year ignited strong resentment at the presence of 47,000 U.S. troops in Japan -- an issue the JCP has exploited.
While vaguely advocating the consolidation and reduction of U.S. military bases in Japan, the other parties basically support the Japan-U.S. military alliance.
Founded in 1922, the JCP was repeatedly suppressed by the authorities in the years up to World War Two, only to be revived by its few remaining members after the war.
The JCP, which refuses to accept campaign funds from the government or donations from business, is financed mainly by sales of the party newspaper Akahata or "Red Flag".
